title: Performance Enhancing Drugs
tagline: Hormone classes, axis pathways, and high-yield agents — taught for medicine, not a how-to guide.
disclaimer: Educational pharmacology and physiology only. Abuse carries serious medical, legal, and sporting consequences.

steroid.label: Steroid hormones
steroid.summary: Lipid-derived, ring-structured hormones made on demand rather than stored — they cross the target cell membrane and act on intracellular nuclear receptors, so the output is gene transcription and the effect takes hours and outlasts the dose.
steroid.where: Nuclear hormone receptors in cytoplasm/nucleus of target cells. Classic axes: HPG (gonadal), adrenal (cortisol), mineralocorticoid.

agents.name: Testosterone
agents.where: Androgen receptor (nuclear) — the body's own androgen ligand acting on skeletal muscle, bone, marrow erythropoiesis and CNS
agents.pathway: HPG axis · Leydig cells
agents.pedNote: Exogenous forms (enanthate, cypionate, undecanoate, gels) prolong half-life; suppresses HPG via negative feedback. Detection is the hard case, because the drug is identical to the molecule the body already makes: screening flags a urinary testosterone/epitestosterone ratio above 4 or a shift in the athlete's own steroid profile on the biological passport, and carbon-isotope-ratio mass spectrometry confirms it — pharmaceutical testosterone is built from plant sterols and carries a lighter ¹³C signature than the endogenous hormone.
agents.pearl: Only ~2% circulates free — the rest is bound to SHBG and albumin, so anything that lowers SHBG (17α-alkylated orals, insulin resistance) drives total and free testosterone apart on the same panel.

agents.name: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
agents.where: Androgen receptor — prostate, skin, hair follicles
agents.pathway: 5α-reductase on testosterone
agents.pedNote: DHT itself is rarely injected, but 5α-reductase inhibition matters for doping: finasteride was WADA-banned 2005–2008 as a masking agent because it distorts the urinary steroid profile and impaired AAS detection.
agents.pearl: Type 2 5α-reductase is the prostate and scalp-follicle isoenzyme finasteride blocks; congenital deficiency gives 46,XY undervirilized external genitalia with normally formed Wolffian structures (epididymis, vas, seminal vesicles), because those depend on testosterone rather than DHT.

agents.name: Estradiol
agents.where: Estrogen receptors (ERα/ERβ) as the native agonist — bone, CV, breast, feedback on HPG
agents.pathway: Aromatase on testosterone/androstenedione
agents.pedNote: Estradiol is the by-product athletes try to control, not a doping agent itself: aromatization of high-dose AAS is what drives gynecomastia and on-cycle water retention, which is why E2 is monitored alongside testosterone on cycle.
agents.pearl: In men roughly 80% of circulating estradiol comes from peripheral aromatization of testosterone — mostly in adipose tissue — rather than from the testis, which is why higher body fat means more estrogenic side effect from the same testosterone dose.

agents.name: Cortisol
agents.where: Glucocorticoid receptor — anti-inflammatory, gluconeogenesis, immunosuppression
agents.pathway: HPA: CRH → ACTH → adrenal cortex
agents.pedNote: Systemic glucocorticoids are abused in-competition for analgesia, euphoria, and training through injury — WADA S9 bans oral/injectable/rectal routes in-competition. Not anabolic — catabolic to muscle at supraphysiologic exposure.
agents.pearl: Exogenous glucocorticoids ↓ ACTH/CRH via negative feedback — adrenal suppression risk.

agents.name: Aldosterone
agents.where: Mineralocorticoid receptor — kidney distal tubule Na⁺ retention
agents.pathway: Adrenal zona glomerulosa · RAAS
agents.pedNote: Indirectly relevant via fluid balance; fludrocortisone rarely abused.
agents.pearl: Spironolactone blocks MR — also anti-androgen (gynecomastia).

agents.name: Nandrolone
agents.where: Androgen receptor — skeletal muscle, bone and marrow (it was a clinical anemia drug); unlike the DHT-derived orals here it is a non-17α-alkylated 19-nor given only by injection, so there is no alkyl hepatic burden
agents.pathway: Testosterone-derived · 19-nor (C19 methyl removed), injected as a long decanoate ester
agents.pedNote: Long metabolite detection window; classic 'Deca' in doping literature.
agents.pearl: 19-nor structure: 5α-reduction gives 5α-dihydronandrolone, which is WEAKER at AR — the opposite of testosterone→DHT, hence androgen-sparing. Aromatizes weakly (~20% of T) and is a potent progesterone-receptor agonist.

agents.name: Stanozolol
agents.where: Androgen receptor — skeletal muscle and bone; the only agent here sold as an aqueous microcrystalline injection as well as a tablet, and 17α-alkylated either way, so hepatic strain follows both routes
agents.pathway: DHT-derived · pyrazole-fused A-ring, 17α-alkylated oral
agents.pedNote: Ben Johnson, Seoul 1988 — the positive that made stanozolol notorious; today's assay targets the 3'-hydroxystanozolol metabolite, which persists in urine long after the parent drug clears.
agents.pearl: Non-aromatizable — the fused pyrazole replaces the 3-keto group aromatase needs, so no gynecomastia; the marked SHBG drop and HDL crash are the trade-off

agents.name: Oxandrolone
agents.where: Androgen receptor in skeletal muscle — a 17α-alkylated oral whose androgenic score (24) is the lowest of the synthetics here, which is where the "mild" reputation comes from
agents.pathway: DHT-derived · 2-oxa A-ring, 17α-alkylated oral
agents.pedNote: Held FDA approval for weight gain after extensive surgery, chronic infection or severe trauma — withdrawn in 2023 for reasons of safety and efficacy; abused for lean gain without much water retention.
agents.pearl: 17α-alkylated like the other orals, but the 2-oxa A-ring and largely renal excretion make it among the least hepatotoxic of the class — "milder," not harmless.

agents.name: Boldenone
agents.where: Androgen receptor — muscle, bone; the Δ1 double bond leaves it aromatizing at roughly half testosterone's rate
agents.pathway: Testosterone Δ1 analogue · aromatizes to estrogen
agents.pedNote: Veterinary "Equipoise" (horses), long undecylenate ester; trace boldenone occurs endogenously and via contaminated meat, so positives need IRMS carbon-isotope confirmation.
agents.pearl: Screening targets the long-term urinary metabolite 5β-androst-1-en-17β-ol-3-one rather than the parent drug, which clears far sooner — which is why the detection window runs to months.

agents.name: Tamoxifen
agents.where: Estrogen receptor antagonist (breast) / partial agonist elsewhere
agents.pathway: Blocks estradiol at ER — not a steroid hormone itself
agents.pedNote: Post-cycle therapy — as a SERM it blocks estrogen at the receptor in the hypothalamus/pituitary, raising LH/FSH to restart suppressed endogenous testosterone. WADA S4.2 (anti-estrogenic substances), banned at all times; not a masking agent and not anabolic.
agents.pearl: SERM: antagonist in breast, agonist in bone/uterus — know tissue selectivity.

agents.name: Anastrozole
agents.where: Aromatase (CYP19A1) itself — the enzyme, not a receptor; blocked wherever it sits, adipose, bone, brain and gonad alike
agents.pathway: Aromatization blockade — peripheral tissues and gonad alike
agents.pedNote: Reduces estrogen during high-testosterone abuse; bone density risk long-term.
agents.pearl: Non-steroidal AI; lowers E2 without blocking ER directly.

peptide.label: Peptide hormones
peptide.summary: Amino-acid chains. Bind cell-surface receptors → second messengers (cAMP, JAK-STAT, tyrosine kinase cascades). Cannot orally absorb intact — injected or inhaled (some).
peptide.where: Plasma membrane receptors on target cells. Often secreted from pituitary, hypothalamus, kidney, pancreas.

agents.name: Growth hormone (GH)
agents.where: GH receptor (JAK2/STAT) — liver, bone, muscle; ↑ IGF-1
agents.pathway: Somatotropic axis — GH itself, released by anterior pituitary somatotrophs under GHRH (+) and somatostatin (−)
agents.pedNote: rhGH abuse for lipolysis + IGF-1-mediated anabolism; short detection window — caught by the 22 kDa isoform ratio test or the IGF-1 / P-III-NP biomarker test.
agents.pearl: Secreted in pulses, mostly in slow-wave sleep — a random GH level is uninterpretable, which is why IGF-1 is measured instead.

agents.name: IGF-1
agents.where: IGF-1 receptor (tyrosine kinase) — muscle, bone
agents.pathway: Liver + local production downstream of GH
agents.pedNote: IGF-1 LR3 and DES(1-3) variants abused for direct muscle anabolism — both are edited at the IGFBP-3 binding site, so they escape the binding proteins that buffer native IGF-1 and circulate free.
agents.pearl: Structurally homologous to proinsulin — which is why it cross-activates the insulin receptor and can drive hypoglycemia.

agents.name: Erythropoietin (EPO)
agents.where: EPO receptor (JAK2) on erythroid progenitors in bone marrow
agents.pathway: Hypoxia → HIF → renal EPO → ↑ RBC mass
agents.pedNote: rhEPO / darbepoetin ↑ hematocrit → endurance; thrombosis risk.
agents.pearl: Active rhEPO abuse: ↑ hematocrit/Hgb WITH elevated reticulocytes; reticulocytes fall after stopping (OFF-score / Athlete Biological Passport).

agents.name: Insulin
agents.where: Insulin receptor (tyrosine kinase) — muscle, fat, liver
agents.pathway: Glucose sensing → β-cell secretion
agents.pedNote: Abused with GH/IGF for anabolism; fatal hypoglycemia risk.
agents.pearl: The dominant glucose-lowering hormone; glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol and GH are the four counter-regulatory hormones opposing it.

agents.name: hCG
agents.where: LH/CG receptor on Leydig cells — same receptor as LH, but a ~24 h half-life versus LH's ~30 min
agents.pathway: Mimics LH in HPG axis
agents.pedNote: Used post-cycle to restart endogenous testicular testosterone after AAS suppression; prohibited in males only and detected by immunoassay for intact hCG.
agents.pearl: α subunit like LH/FSH/TSH; β subunit unique — clinical immunoassays key on β-hCG, but doping control requires an assay for the intact α/β dimer, the only biologically active form.

agents.name: ACTH
agents.where: MC2 receptor on adrenal cortex → cortisol
agents.pathway: CRH → ACTH → cortisol
agents.pedNote: Rare direct abuse; tetracosactide (ACTH analogue) in doping history.
agents.pearl: ACTH 1–39; shorter fragments used diagnostically (stimulation test).

agents.name: GnRH
agents.where: GnRH receptor on pituitary gonadotrophs → LH/FSH pulse
agents.pathway: Hypothalamic apex of the HPG axis — pulsatile GnRH → pituitary LH/FSH
agents.pedNote: Continuous GnRH agonists paradoxically suppress LH/FSH (downregulation).
agents.pearl: Pulsatile = stimulate; continuous infusion = chemical castration (prostate CA).

agents.name: LH / FSH
agents.where: Gonadal receptors — Leydig (LH), Sertoli/granulosa (FSH)
agents.pathway: Pituitary gonadotroph tier of the HPG axis — pulsatile GnRH drives LH/FSH release, restrained by gonadal steroid feedback, with inhibin B selectively suppressing FSH
agents.pedNote: Rarely bought as PEDs themselves — hCG stands in for LH at the same Leydig-cell receptor with a far longer half-life, and recombinant FSH is expensive and only adds spermatogenesis recovery.
agents.pearl: LH drives testosterone; FSH drives spermatogenesis / folliculogenesis.

agents.name: GHRP / GHRH analogs
agents.where: GHRH receptor or ghrelin/GH secretagogue receptor → ↑ GH pulse
agents.pathway: Upstream of GH axis
agents.pedNote: CJC-1295 and ipamorelin are grey-market research chemicals; tesamorelin is an FDA-approved GHRH analogue (Egrifta, for HIV lipodystrophy) diverted to the same use. Because the GH released is the athlete's own, the 22 kDa isoform-ratio test stays normal — so detection leans on catching the secretagogue peptide itself by LC-MS/MS, or on the IGF-1 / P-III-NP biomarker test, which reads GH action regardless of source.
agents.pearl: Work by amplifying endogenous GH pulses rather than replacing GH protein.

agents.name: Glucagon
agents.where: Glucagon receptor — hepatocyte glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis
agents.pathway: Pancreatic α-cell counter-regulatory arm — opposes insulin at the liver
agents.pedNote: Not performance-enhancing; know for hypoglycemia rescue contrast.
agents.pearl: Glucagon is the antidote in β-blocker overdose — it raises cardiac cAMP through its own Gs-coupled receptor, bypassing the blocked β1.

amine.label: Amine hormones
amine.summary: Derived from tyrosine or tryptophan. Catecholamines and thyroid hormones — faster signaling or iodinated amines acting on nuclear receptors.
amine.where: Catecholamines: GPCRs (α/β adrenergic). Thyroid hormones: nuclear receptors (TR) after cellular uptake.

agents.name: Epinephrine
agents.where: α1, α2, β1, β2 — direct, nonselective agonist across α and β receptors; heart, bronchi, vasculature
agents.pathway: Sympathoadrenal — adrenal medullary hormone released into blood
agents.pedNote: WADA S6 stimulant in-competition — but expressly exempt in local administration (nasal, ophthalmic, or with a local anaesthetic). Not a chronic PED; the endogenous stress catecholamine.
agents.pearl: Epinephrine reversal: after α-blockade its unopposed β2 vasodilation flips the pressor response into a fall in BP — does not happen with norepinephrine, which has minimal β2.

agents.name: Norepinephrine
agents.where: α1, α2 > β1 — vasoconstriction; minimal β2. ↑MAP with reflex bradycardia, CO unchanged or ↓
agents.pathway: Postganglionic sympathetic neurotransmitter (~20% of adrenal medullary output)
agents.pedNote: Not itself abused — but it is the transmitter that amphetamine and ephedrine release, and the α1 pressor effect behind their hypertensive risk
agents.pearl: Norepinephrine extravasation from a peripheral line causes local vasoconstriction and skin necrosis — infiltrate the site with phentolamine, an α-blocker.

agents.name: Dopamine
agents.where: D1–D5 receptors — renal/mesenteric vasodilation at low infusion, β1 then α1 as the rate climbs; given IV it does NOT cross the blood–brain barrier. Precursor to NE/Epi.
agents.pathway: CNS motor/reward; prolactin inhibition (Tuberoinfundibular)
agents.pedNote: Bromocriptine/cabergoline (dopamine agonists) suppress prolactin on cycles.
agents.pearl: "Renal-dose" dopamine is a myth — randomized trials showed low-dose infusion does not prevent acute kidney injury or death, so it is no longer recommended for renal protection.

agents.name: Thyroxine (T4)
agents.where: Nuclear thyroid receptors after 5'-deiodinase → T3
agents.pathway: HPT axis: TRH → TSH → follicular cells; ~100% of T4 is thyroidal in origin
agents.pedNote: Exogenous levothyroxine abused for weight loss / metabolic rate.
agents.pearl: T4 has a ~7-day half-life (weekly dosing possible) and is >99.9% protein-bound — a reservoir, not the active ligand

agents.name: Triiodothyronine (T3)
agents.where: Nuclear thyroid receptors (TRα/TRβ) — sets basal metabolic rate; upregulates cardiac β1 sensitivity
agents.pathway: Peripheral conversion of T4 or direct secretion
agents.pedNote: Liothyronine cuts — catabolic if overdosed, arrhythmia risk. Labs trap: suppressed TSH with LOW free T4 (T3-only user), unlike T4 misuse which raises free T4
agents.pearl: Roughly 3–4× more potent than T4 with a ~1-day half-life — the active ligand at the receptor, not the reservoir

agents.name: Amphetamine / methylphenidate
agents.where: ↑ synaptic catecholamines — amphetamine by DAT/NET transporter reversal + VMAT2 vesicular release; methylphenidate by DAT/NET reuptake blockade only
agents.pathway: No hormone axis — amphetamine and methylphenidate act on the presynaptic terminal itself, so the effect depends on the neuron's own catecholamine stores rather than on any endocrine signal
agents.pedNote: WADA S6, in-competition only and TUE-eligible for ADHD — abused for focus, aggression and blunted fatigue perception.
agents.pearl: Renal handling is pH-dependent — alkaline urine reabsorbs amphetamine and prolongs it, acidic urine speeds clearance.

agents.name: Clenbuterol
agents.where: β2 receptors — bronchodilation, skeletal muscle anabolic signal (debated)
agents.pathway: Direct receptor agonism with no hormone axis upstream — the effect does not depend on endogenous catecholamine stores, unlike the releasers
agents.pedNote: Veterinary bronchodilator abused for cutting; tremor, tachycardia, hypokalemia. Prohibited at all times (classed with anabolic agents); ≤5 ng/mL urine reported as Atypical — the meat-contamination defence
agents.pearl: Long β2 action: ~26–37 h half-life gives a urinary detection window of weeks, unlike the minute-scale catecholamines

agents.name: Ephedrine / pseudoephedrine
agents.where: α and β receptors on vasculature, heart and bronchi — but reached mostly indirectly, since ephedrine is carried into the sympathetic nerve terminal by NET and displaces stored NE
agents.pathway: Presynaptic NE release + weak direct α/β agonism (mixed-acting)
agents.pedNote: In-competition only: ephedrine prohibited >10 µg/mL urine, pseudoephedrine >150 µg/mL; hemorrhagic stroke and MI risk (ephedra supplements FDA-banned 2004)
agents.pearl: Pseudoephedrine is ephedrine's diastereomer — differs at one of two stereocentres, giving roughly a third the pressor potency while keeping useful nasal decongestion, so it decongests with less cardiovascular and CNS stimulation. Both are meth precursors: the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act of 2005 (retail rules from September 2006) keeps them behind the counter or in a locked cabinet — at any registered seller, not just pharmacies — with photo ID and a logbook.

agents.name: Caffeine
agents.where: Competitive antagonist at A1/A2A adenosine receptors (CNS) — lowers perceived effort
agents.pathway: CNS adenosine A1/A2A antagonism — not catecholaminergic
agents.pedNote: Not WADA-prohibited (monitored only), but NCAA bans it above 15 µg/mL urinary — ~2–4% gain in time-trial performance at 3–6 mg/kg (open-ended time-to-exhaustion tests report far larger percentages for the same dose)
agents.pearl: Cleared almost entirely by CYP1A2 — smoking roughly halves its half-life while pregnancy and oral contraceptives roughly double it, so the same dose is not the same exposure.

studyPath.title: Clinical & detection
studyPath.subtitle: Labs, risks, what you see in practice

items.name: Testosterone esters
items.risk: HPG suppression, polycythemia, dyslipidemia, acne, aggression

items.name: Stanozolol / oxandrolone
items.risk: Hepatotoxicity (cholestasis, peliosis); HDL crash with rising LDL

items.name: SARMs (ostarine, etc.)
items.risk: HPG suppression; documented cholestatic liver injury (ostarine, LGD-4033, RAD-140 case reports); FDA warns of heart attack and stroke; prohibited at all times under WADA S1.2

items.name: hCG
items.risk: Gynecomastia; prohibited in males only, detected by immunoassay for intact hCG

items.name: Altitude tents / hypoxia
items.risk: Not prohibited by WADA — its ethics panel called it contrary to the spirit of sport but it was deliberately left off the List; some national bodies restrict it. Physiologic cost is disrupted sleep and dehydration; it mimics natural acclimatization

items.name: HIF stabilizers (roxadustat, daprodustat)
items.moa: Blocks prolyl hydroxylase → HIF survives → ↑ the athlete's own EPO
items.risk: Same hyperviscosity and thrombosis as rhEPO, but no recombinant protein to find — prohibited at all times as HIF activating agents (WADA S2.1); caught by detecting the parent drug and by the passport

items.name: Carbon monoxide rebreathing
items.moa: Repeated low-dose CO inhalation as a hypoxic stimulus to raise haemoglobin mass
items.risk: Hypoxic injury and dose error with a colourless, odourless gas; non-diagnostic use added to the Prohibited List as method M1.4 on 1 January 2026 — the boundary case that altitude tents are not

items.name: Aromatase inhibitors / SERMs
items.risk: AIs: bone loss, arthralgia, adverse lipid shift; SERMs: hot flushes, thromboembolism; tamoxifen additionally raises endometrial cancer risk in women (raloxifene does not)

items.name: Plasma expanders
items.risk: Fluid overload, coagulopathy, renal injury (hydroxyethyl starch carries an FDA boxed warning); defeats the blood screen rather than being caught by it — detected directly in urine

labs.low: Hemodilution — IV plasma expanders (dextran, hydroxyethyl starch, albumin, mannitol) or saline infusion used to mask blood doping; also the withdrawal phase of autologous transfusion, and ordinary plasma-volume shifts

labs.high: Active rhEPO / darbepoetin — retics rise while haemoglobin climbs; also haemolysis or marrow recovery
labs.low: Recently stopped rhEPO, or reinfused blood suppressing endogenous EPO — low retics WITH a high haemoglobin is the OFF-score pattern the Athlete Biological Passport flags (recent altitude and plasma-volume shifts are the innocent explanations)

labs.high: SERM or aromatase-inhibitor use in post-cycle therapy (estrogen feedback blocked); otherwise primary gonadal failure — rare in abuse

Exogenous testosterone itself — esters, gel or oral undecanoate — since the assay measures testosterone and the other AAS do not raise it; also hCG, which drives the athlete's own Leydig cells. Either way the giveaway is a high testosterone with a suppressed LH. In doping control a high result is not the finding: the follow-up is the urinary testosterone/epitestosterone ratio and carbon-isotope-ratio mass spectrometry, which tells pharmaceutical testosterone from the athlete's own.
labs.low: Post-cycle crash — and active use of a non-testosterone AAS or SARM (stanozolol, oxandrolone, ostarine), which suppresses endogenous testosterone while staying invisible to the testosterone assay: low T with low LH. Cross-reactivity on the immunoassay is real but small and does not rescue the pattern — boldenone runs about 7% and nandrolone (19-nortestosterone) about 2%, enough to falsely raise a woman's result but nowhere near enough to lift a suppressed man's testosterone out of the low range. LC-MS/MS is the confirmatory method.

labs.high: rhGH abuse; also GH secretagogues (CJC-1295, ipamorelin) pushing endogenous GH — the isoform test misses rhGH once its short window closes and never sees secretagogues at all, since the GH released is the athlete's own, which is why the slower biomarker test reads IGF-1 + P-III-NP; acromegaly is the non-drug cause
High free T4 with suppressed TSH = levothyroxine (T4) misuse; high TSH with low free T4 = primary hypothyroidism
labs.low: Suppressed TSH with LOW free T4 = liothyronine (T3-only) misuse — reads as central hypothyroidism on a screening panel until a free T3 is added, and it will be high

labs.high: 17α-alkylated orals — bland cholestasis, so bilirubin climbs while ALP stays normal or barely raised; intense training or rhabdomyolysis releases AST/ALT from muscle instead — a high CK with AST above ALT points to muscle, not liver

risks: Cardiovascular: MI, stroke, cardiomyopathy, hypertension, dyslipidemia; arterial and venous thrombosis from EPO/transfusion-driven hyperviscosity
Hepatic: cholestasis, peliosis, tumors with 17α-alkylated orals

Endocrine: infertility, gynecomastia, adrenal/gonadal axis suppression; rhGH → acromegalic change (jaw, hands, feet), insulin resistance and overt diabetes; T3/T4 misuse → iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis with muscle catabolism
Psychiatric: irritability, mania, depression on withdrawal

Renal / metabolic: rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuric acute kidney injury, diuretic-induced hypovolemia and electrolyte collapse (hypokalemia — β2 agonists like clenbuterol, and insulin, also drive K⁺ intracellularly), severe hypoglycemia (insulin)
Infectious: HIV, hepatitis B and C, injection-site abscess and endocarditis from shared or non-sterile injecting (AAS, rhGH, rhEPO, insulin)

Androgenic / musculoskeletal: acne, male-pattern hair loss, prostate growth; irreversible virilization in women (voice deepening, clitoromegaly, hirsutism); premature epiphyseal closure and permanently reduced adult height in adolescents, driven by the aromatized estrogen; tendon rupture

pathways.title: HPG axis (gonadal)
pathways.subtitle: GnRH pulse → sex steroids
pathways.orientation: The hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis converts pulsatile GnRH into LH/FSH, then into testosterone and its metabolites. This is the axis exogenous androgens shut down.

steps.label: FSH (released alongside LH, not after it)
steps.hint: Pituitary — co-secreted with LH from the same gonadotroph under the same GnRH signal, not downstream of LH; acts on Sertoli/granulosa for spermatogenesis/follicles

steps.label: Testosterone (LH-driven, not FSH)
steps.hint: Leydig cell steroid — negative feedback on HPG

steps.label: Estradiol (the other branch off testosterone)
steps.hint: Aromatase metabolite — a parallel fate of testosterone, not made from DHT (5α-reduced steroids are not aromatase substrates); drives feedback + gynecomastia risk

forkQuiz.prompt: GnRH is released from the…
forkQuiz.after: Pulsatile GnRH is required — continuous exposure suppresses LH/FSH.

forkQuiz.prompt: LH acts primarily on…
forkQuiz.after: LH → ↑ testosterone synthesis in Leydig cells.

forkQuiz.prompt: Testosterone converts to DHT via…
forkQuiz.after: Finasteride blocks 5α-reductase — ↓ DHT.

forkQuiz.prompt: Exogenous testosterone suppresses LH/FSH through…
forkQuiz.after: HPG shutdown → testicular atrophy, infertility until recovery.

pathways.title: GH–IGF axis
pathways.subtitle: GHRH / somatostatin → GH → IGF-1
pathways.orientation: Growth hormone is pulsatile from the anterior pituitary; IGF-1 from the liver is the stable downstream signal. rhGH abuse targets this loop.

steps.label: GHRH
steps.hint: Hypothalamic stimulator of GH release — the pituitary also answers to somatostatin, its inhibitory opposite, so GH output is the balance of the two

forkQuiz.prompt: GH is secreted from the…
forkQuiz.after: Posterior pituitary stores ADH/oxytocin — not GH.

forkQuiz.prompt: The best stable blood marker of excess GH is…
forkQuiz.after: GH is pulsatile; IGF-1 integrates exposure.

forkQuiz.prompt: Somatostatin acts to…
forkQuiz.after: Octreotide mimics somatostatin — used in acromegaly.

forkQuiz.prompt: Most of the IGF-1 circulating in blood is produced by…
forkQuiz.after: GH drives hepatic IGF-1 — that is the endocrine pool; muscle IGF-1 acts locally.

pathways.title: HPA axis
pathways.subtitle: CRH → ACTH → cortisol
pathways.orientation: Stress and inflammation drive CRH → ACTH → cortisol. Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress the entire axis — the source of the adrenal-insufficiency risk on abrupt withdrawal. They sit in WADA S9, banned in-competition by oral, injectable and rectal routes for analgesia and euphoria; the masking agents are the S5 diuretics and plasma expanders.

forkQuiz.prompt: ACTH is released from the…
forkQuiz.after: CRH from hypothalamus stimulates ACTH release.

forkQuiz.prompt: Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress ACTH via…
forkQuiz.after: Risk of adrenal insufficiency if stopped abruptly after chronic use.

forkQuiz.prompt: ACTH acts on which layer of the adrenal gland to drive cortisol output?
forkQuiz.after: Fasciculata makes glucocorticoids. Glomerulosa makes aldosterone under angiotensin II, reticularis makes androgens, medulla makes catecholamines.

forkQuiz.prompt: Cortisol raises blood glucose mainly by driving…
forkQuiz.after: Cortisol is gluconeogenic — it mobilizes amino acids and glycerol into new glucose, sparing fuel for the stress response, while also blunting inflammation.

pathways.title: Thyroid axis
pathways.subtitle: TRH → TSH → T4 → T3
pathways.orientation: Thyroid hormone sets metabolic rate. T3 abuse mimics hyperthyroidism — weight loss at the cost of cardiac and muscle risk.

forkQuiz.prompt: T3 is more biologically active because…
forkQuiz.after: T3 binds the nuclear thyroid receptor with about ten times the affinity of T4 — that is what makes it the active ligand, not its half-life (T4 actually lasts far longer, ~7 days vs ~1 day). Affinity at the receptor is not the same thing as clinical potency, which is quoted lower. Most circulating T3 is made outside the thyroid, by 5'-deiodinase stripping an iodine from T4.

forkQuiz.prompt: Exogenous T3 suppresses…
forkQuiz.after: Endogenous thyrotoxicosis: ↓ TSH with ↑ T3 and a normal-to-↑ T4. Exogenous T3 alone: ↓ TSH with ↑ T3 but ↓ T4 — suppressed TSH shuts down the only gland that makes T4.

forkQuiz.prompt: TSH acts directly on…
forkQuiz.after: TSH from the anterior pituitary binds follicular cells, driving iodide uptake, thyroglobulin iodination, and T4 release. Parafollicular (C) cells sit in the same gland but answer to calcium, not TSH — they secrete calcitonin. Sustained TSH drive is also what enlarges the gland into a goiter.

forkQuiz.prompt: T4 is called a prohormone because…
forkQuiz.answer: It is converted to T3 in tissues
options: It is converted to T3 in tissues
It binds the T3 receptor tightly
It is stored in the pituitary gland
It is released in response to ACTH
forkQuiz.after: The thyroid ships mostly T4, which does little on its own; peripheral 5'-deiodinase strips one iodine to yield T3, the ligand that actually drives the nuclear receptor. Gland makes the precursor, tissues do the activating — that is the definition of a prohormone, and it is why T4 dosing depends on intact peripheral conversion.

pathways.title: Erythropoiesis
pathways.subtitle: Hypoxia → EPO → RBC mass
pathways.orientation: Kidney EPO is the hormone arm of oxygen delivery. rhEPO and blood doping raise hematocrit — endurance benefit with thrombosis risk.

forkQuiz.prompt: EPO is produced mainly in the…
forkQuiz.after: Small fraction from liver; renal failure → anemia.

forkQuiz.prompt: EPO acts on erythroid progenitors via…
forkQuiz.after: JAK2 pathway — overlap with polycythemia vera mutations.

forkQuiz.prompt: In plentiful oxygen HIF is short-lived, because prolyl hydroxylases tag it for…
forkQuiz.after: Prolyl hydroxylases use O₂ as a substrate, so in normoxia they hydroxylate HIF-1α, the VHL complex ubiquitinates it and the proteasome destroys it within minutes. Low O₂ stalls the hydroxylases, HIF survives — that is what the HIF-stabilization step in the chain means — and it switches on the EPO gene.

forkQuiz.prompt: When EPO drive on the marrow rises, the lab value that climbs first is…
forkQuiz.after: Retics are the newly released immature RBCs — up within days, while hematocrit lags weeks behind. High hemoglobin with low retics is the post-EPO withdrawal pattern the Athlete Biological Passport flags.

pathways.title: Steroid synthesis (overview)
pathways.subtitle: Cholesterol → androgens / cortisol / aldosterone
pathways.orientation: All steroid hormones share cholesterol-derived scaffolding. Knowing the branches explains why enzymes like aromatase and 5α-reductase matter on cycles.

steps.label: Pregnenolone
steps.hint: First steroid hormone — Δ5 pathway hub, common precursor to every branch

steps.label: Testosterone (androgen branch — 5α-reduces on to DHT, aromatizes to estradiol)
steps.hint: Leydig cells — the adrenal zona reticularis makes DHEA and androstenedione, which are converted to testosterone peripherally

steps.label: Cortisol — separate branch, off 17-OH progesterone
steps.hint: NOT downstream of testosterone: 17-OH progesterone → 11-deoxycortisol (21-hydroxylase) → cortisol (11β-hydroxylase), zona fasciculata, ACTH-driven

steps.label: Aldosterone — third branch, not made from cortisol
steps.hint: Third parallel branch — not downstream of cortisol. Progesterone → deoxycorticosterone → aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2), driven by angiotensin II and K⁺, with ACTH only a minor contributor

forkQuiz.prompt: The rate-limiting step converting cholesterol to pregnenolone uses…
forkQuiz.after: Also called desmolase — mitochondrial inner membrane.

forkQuiz.prompt: Most of the aromatase activity in a man's body sits in…
forkQuiz.after: Aromatase is concentrated in adipose tissue (also gonad, brain and bone). More body fat means more testosterone converted to estradiol — which is why gynecomastia risk on AAS tracks adiposity.

forkQuiz.prompt: Aldosterone is synthesized in the…
forkQuiz.after: Angiotensin II and K⁺ regulate aldosterone — RAAS.

forkQuiz.prompt: Aldosterone is regulated independently of cortisol because its main drivers are…
forkQuiz.after: Cortisol runs on ACTH from the HPA axis; aldosterone answers to RAAS and plasma potassium instead, with ACTH only a minor contributor. Same gland, same cholesterol backbone, separate control — which is why the two branches move independently.

steroid.title: One molecule, three signals
steroid.blurb: Testosterone and the two enzymes that change what it means.

teach.p: It binds the androgen receptor directly — a nuclear receptor, so the effect is transcriptional. Changes take hours to days and outlast the dose, which is why androgen effects are measured in weeks rather than minutes.

5α-reductase converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, which binds the same androgen receptor far more tightly. The enzyme sits in skin, scalp and prostate — so this is the arm that produces acne, male-pattern hair loss and prostate growth. Skeletal muscle has almost no 5α-reductase and responds to testosterone itself, which is why DHT is the androgenic signal rather than the anabolic one — and why finasteride does not blunt muscle gain.

Aromatase, concentrated in adipose tissue (also gonad, brain and bone), converts testosterone to estradiol, which acts at the estrogen receptor instead. Estrogen in men is not an error: it is required for epiphyseal closure, bone density and normal negative feedback. More body fat means more aromatization — and gynecomastia tracks the estrogen-to-androgen ratio at breast tissue, not estradiol alone.

One molecule yields three signals through two receptors: testosterone and DHT at the androgen receptor, estradiol at the estrogen receptor. Block one fate and you do not redirect the molecule so much as shift the balance between the signals that remain — the entire reason the anti-estrogens later in this module exist, and why they cost what they cost.

steroid.title: The adrenal steroids answer to different axes
steroid.blurb: Same backbone, different controllers, and only one of them fights the androgens.

teach.p: Cortisol and aldosterone share the steroid backbone but come from the adrenal cortex, not the gonads — and they take orders from entirely different upstream signals.

teach.h: Cortisol runs on the HPA axis
teach.p: CRH from the hypothalamus drives ACTH from the pituitary, which drives cortisol from the adrenal cortex. Cortisol is catabolic — it breaks tissue down to liberate substrate, tearing down the lean mass androgens build. Note the mechanism, though: anabolic steroids build muscle by agonising the androgen receptor — more protein synthesis, satellite-cell recruitment, and a push of muscle precursor cells toward myogenic rather than fat lineage — not primarily by blocking cortisol.

Aldosterone comes from the zona glomerulosa and is driven mainly by angiotensin II and potassium, only minimally by ACTH. It retains sodium and wastes potassium — a volume and electrolyte hormone, not a growth one. Cortisol can bind the mineralocorticoid receptor too, but 11β-HSD2 in the distal nephron converts it to inactive cortisone. That protection is local and saturable: knock the enzyme out (liquorice, apparent mineralocorticoid excess) or flood it (ectopic ACTH) and cortisol drives the receptor exactly like aldosterone.

Identical chemical class, different control axes — HPA for cortisol, RAAS for aldosterone, HPG for the androgens — and only cortisol opposes the androgens on lean tissue. The axes do talk: sustained cortisol suppresses GnRH and LH.

steroid.title: Synthetic AAS — what got changed, and what it cost
steroid.blurb: Each synthetic androgen is testosterone or DHT with a structural edit — and every edit has a price.

teach.p: Plain testosterone taken orally is largely destroyed by first-pass hepatic metabolism — and that is only one of the problems a chemist might want to solve. Every synthetic anabolic–androgenic steroid carries a structural edit with a purpose: some to survive first pass and work orally, some to slow release from an injected depot, some to shift the anabolic-to-androgenic balance itself. Each edit carries its own price.

A methyl group at C17α (stanozolol, oxandrolone) hinders hepatic oxidation, letting the molecule survive first pass and work by mouth. The price is hepatotoxicity — cholestasis, transaminase elevation, and with prolonged use peliosis hepatis and hepatic adenoma. Oxandrolone is among the least hepatotoxic of the class — a 2-oxa A-ring and largely renal excretion — and it held an FDA indication for weight gain after extensive surgery, chronic infection or severe trauma until that approval was withdrawn in 2023 for reasons of safety or effectiveness. Least hepatotoxic is not safe: it is still 17α-alkylated and still suppressive. Others in this class do still carry live indications — oxymetholone for the anaemias of deficient red-cell production, danazol for hereditary angioedema.

A different problem needs a different edit. Esterifying the C17β hydroxyl (testosterone enanthate or cypionate, nandrolone decanoate, boldenone undecylenate) makes the molecule lipophilic enough to sit in an oil depot and release over weeks. The ester itself is inert at the receptor — esterases clip it off to liberate the free steroid. For these four the ester buys duration, not oral survival; one ester breaks the pattern, since testosterone undecanoate is lipophilic enough to be taken up by intestinal lymphatics, which is how the only workable oral testosterone dodges first pass.

Nandrolone is 19-nortestosterone — the C19 methyl is gone, which alters receptor binding and adds progestogenic activity. Here is the callback: where testosterone is 5α-reduced to the stronger DHT, nandrolone is 5α-reduced to 5α-dihydronandrolone, a weaker androgen. That mirror image is why it is comparatively kind to scalp and prostate — though the progestogenic arm exacts its own price on libido and breast tissue.

Nandrolone decanoate releases over weeks like the other depots, but its urinary marker 19-norandrosterone stays detectable for months afterwards — one of the longest windows of any agent here. Boldenone, a veterinary Δ1-testosterone injected as the undecylenate ester, still aromatises and so carries estrogenic effects alongside the androgenic ones.

Whatever the edit, exogenous androgen suppresses the HPG axis by negative feedback: LH and FSH fall, endogenous production shuts down, the testes atrophy and spermatogenesis is impaired. Recovery tracks dose, duration and how long the ester keeps releasing — which is why long-acting depots such as nandrolone decanoate, whose progestogenic activity adds gonadotropin suppression of its own, tend to be the slowest to come back.

steroid.title: Manipulating the estrogen arm
steroid.blurb: Not hormones — tools for controlling the aromatase fate from the first lesson.

teach.h: These two are not steroid hormones
teach.p: Tamoxifen is a triphenylethylene, anastrozole a nonsteroidal triazole. They are here because they exist to control the aromatase branch you learned first — levers on the cascade, not participants in it.

A selective estrogen receptor modulator: an antagonist at breast tissue but an agonist at bone and endometrium. That endometrial agonism is why it carries a real cancer signal in women — not a concern for a male user, whose reason for taking it is the breast antagonism that prevents gynecomastia. By blocking estrogen feedback it also raises LH and FSH, which is why it appears in attempts to restart a suppressed axis.

An aromatase inhibitor works one step upstream, preventing the conversion itself and lowering estradiol systemically. It is highly selective for aromatase over other steroidogenic enzymes — what it lacks is tissue selectivity, so there is nothing to spare the bone. Estradiol falls everywhere: bone density suffers, HDL loses its support, and arthralgia is the toxicity that most often stops people taking it.

Return to the first lesson: block aromatase and you do not remove androgen — you remove its counterweight. The androgenic arm, DHT included, now acts unopposed, and everything estrogen was doing for bone, lipids, libido and feedback goes with it. In a man with an intact axis, losing that feedback also raises LH and testosterone, which does raise DHT; in a suppressed user on exogenous androgen, that loop is already switched off. Either way you cannot suppress one arm of the cascade without paying for it on the other.

peptide.title: Why nobody measures growth hormone
peptide.blurb: GH comes in pulses, so a single level tells you nothing — the axis gets read one step downstream instead.

teach.p: Growth hormone is secreted in bursts, most of them during slow-wave sleep, under GHRH from the hypothalamus and held back by somatostatin. Because of that rhythm a single random GH level tells you almost nothing — draw twice in an hour and you can get a peak and a trough from the same healthy person.

teach.h: So the axis is read one step downstream
teach.p: GH acts on the liver through a cytokine-family receptor — not a receptor tyrosine kinase: it has no kinase domain of its own, and instead recruits JAK2, a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase, which phosphorylates STATs — and the liver responds by making IGF-1. IGF-1 circulates bound to IGFBP-3 and ALS, which buffers it into a stable level. That stability is why IGF-1, not GH, is what gets measured.

teach.h: IGF-1 does much of the work — and carries the risk
teach.p: IGF-1 acts at its own receptor tyrosine kinase to drive tissue growth. It is structurally homologous to proinsulin, and it lowers glucose both through its own receptor and by cross-activating the insulin receptor. The black-market variants make that worse by design: LR3 and DES(1-3) are edited precisely where IGF-1 binds IGFBP-3, so they escape the buffering above and circulate free — which is why they carry a real hypoglycaemia risk.

GHRH analogues such as CJC-1295 and ghrelin-receptor (GHS-R1a) agonists such as ipamorelin do not supply GH — they push the pituitary to release more of its own, so the natural pulse pattern is preserved.

teach.h: Which is exactly how the test works
teach.p: Injected recombinant GH is pure 22 kDa and suppresses the body's other isoforms, so the 22 kDa-to-total ratio shifts — that is the isoform differential test, and its window is short. Secretagogues leave the isoform mix looking normal. The slower biomarker test reads IGF-1 and P-III-NP instead, which is why it exists: it catches what the isoform window misses.

peptide.title: Pulse, or shut it down
peptide.blurb: The same hypothalamic peptide either starts the axis or castrates it — timing decides.

teach.p: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone is a hypothalamic decapeptide acting on pituitary gonadotrophs. Everything below it in the reproductive axis takes its orders from this one signal.

Delivered in pulses, GnRH stimulates the pituitary. Delivered continuously, it does the opposite — the receptor downregulates and the axis shuts off. Same molecule, opposite outcome, decided by nothing but the pattern of delivery. That is the basis of chemical castration with leuprolide.

teach.h: The two gonadotropins split the job
teach.p: LH drives Leydig cells to make testosterone. FSH drives Sertoli cells and spermatogenesis. Only the LH arm has a counterpart on the prohibited list — chorionic gonadotropin and LH are banned in males, FSH is not banned at all — which is why hCG is the one to know.

teach.h: hCG is LH with a longer fuse
teach.p: Human chorionic gonadotropin binds the very same receptor as LH, the LH/CG receptor on Leydig cells. What differs is duration: roughly a 24–36 hour half-life against LH's ~20–30 minutes. So it delivers a sustained rather than pulsatile Leydig signal.

teach.h: Why that matters after a cycle
teach.p: Exogenous androgen suppresses the whole axis, so the testes idle. hCG restarts them directly by substituting for the missing LH signal — which is why it appears in post-cycle protocols, and why it is prohibited in males only. It is detected by immunoassay for hCG, the same class of assay as a pregnancy test.

peptide.title: The glucose tug of war
peptide.blurb: Two pancreatic peptides pulling in opposite directions — and the reason one of them is the most dangerous drug here.

teach.p: Insulin is the dominant glucose-lowering hormone. Opposing it are four counter-regulatory hormones — glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol and growth hormone. The redundancy runs one way for a reason: starvation kills slowly, hypoglycaemia kills fast, so the body evolved four ways up and essentially one way down.
Released by β-cells in response to glucose, insulin acts through a receptor tyrosine kinase on muscle, fat and liver — driving uptake and storage, and blocking breakdown.

From the pancreatic α-cells, glucagon acts on hepatocytes to run glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. It is not a performance drug — it is here as the counterweight, and as the rescue given when someone has driven their glucose too low to treat by mouth.
It is stacked with GH and IGF-1 for anabolism — the same nutrient-partitioning machinery that stores glucose also drives amino acids into muscle.

teach.h: And why it is the fastest killer in this course
teach.p: Most of the agents here kill slowly, over years of exposure — and the few that kill fast, like amphetamine in the heat or EPO-driven thrombosis, need bad luck or a bad day. Insulin does not: a modest dosing error drops glucose within minutes in an otherwise healthy person. The brain holds essentially no fuel of its own, and there is no antidote that switches insulin off — the treatment is substrate: IV dextrose, or glucagon if there is no line, and glucagon works only while there is still liver glycogen to mobilise. That combination, not its anabolic effect, is the fact worth carrying out of this lesson.

peptide.title: Oxygen, stress, and detecting a fingerprint
peptide.blurb: When the drug is gone before the test, you look for what it did instead.

teach.h: EPO is an oxygen sensor's output
teach.p: Low tissue oxygen stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor, which drives the kidney to make and release erythropoietin. EPO acts on marrow erythroid progenitors through EPOR/JAK2, raising red cell mass — and with it oxygen delivery, which is the entire endurance rationale for abusing it.
More red cells means thicker blood. The signature risk of recombinant EPO abuse is thrombosis, and it is not theoretical.

teach.h: Reading the fingerprint, not the drug
teach.p: Recombinant EPO clears from urine within days, so the direct test — isoelectric focusing or SAR-PAGE, separating the recombinant glycoform from the athlete's own EPO — only works if the sample lands inside a narrow window. The complementary approach is to read what the drug did to the marrow. During active use, reticulocytes are elevated while haemoglobin climbs. After stopping, reticulocytes fall below baseline while haemoglobin stays high — a suppressed marrow coasting on cells it already made.

High haemoglobin together with suppressed reticulocytes is a pattern the body rarely produces on its own — the innocent explanations are a recent altitude camp or a plasma-volume shift such as dehydration, which is exactly why athletes must declare altitude exposure and why a flagged passport goes to an expert panel rather than straight to a sanction. The Athlete Biological Passport tracks these markers over time in each individual, so the evidence is a departure from that athlete's own baseline, which can support a sanction on its own or trigger a targeted direct test for the drug itself.

Rather than injecting a glucocorticoid, ACTH drives the adrenal cortex to make more of the athlete's own cortisol — the same CRH → ACTH → cortisol axis, entered one step up. Corticotrophins are prohibited at all times.

amine.title: One assembly line, three hormones
amine.blurb: Dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline are consecutive steps — what separates them is which receptors they reach.

teach.p: Tyrosine becomes DOPA, DOPA becomes dopamine, dopamine becomes norepinephrine, and norepinephrine becomes epinephrine. Each one is the raw material for the next, so these are not three unrelated molecules but three stops on a single production line.

teach.h: Receptor reach is what separates them
teach.p: Epinephrine is a direct, nonselective agonist across α and β receptors. Norepinephrine has strong α and β1 activity but minimal β2. That one gap is responsible for most of the difference between them.

teach.h: Follow the β2 gap into the haemodynamics
teach.p: With no β2 vasodilation anywhere to blunt it, norepinephrine raises mean arterial pressure through unopposed α1 vasoconstriction. The baroreceptors answer with reflex bradycardia, and that slowing — together with the rise in afterload — offsets the β1 inotropy, so cardiac output typically stays flat or falls even though the pressure is up. Expecting β1 to raise output here is the classic error.

Given intravenously, dopamine does not cross the blood–brain barrier — the reason Parkinson's is treated with L-DOPA rather than dopamine itself. Its effect climbs through receptor classes as the infusion rate rises: renal and mesenteric vasodilation low, β1 inotropy in the middle, α1 vasoconstriction high.

Block the α receptors and give epinephrine, and its β2 vasodilation is left unopposed: the expected rise in blood pressure inverts into a fall. Do the same with norepinephrine and nothing inverts — there is barely any β2 to be unmasked. One receptor's worth of difference, visible at the bedside.

amine.title: The reservoir and the ligand
amine.blurb: T4 is storage, T3 is signal — and knowing which is which is how you read the labs.

teach.p: Essentially all circulating T4 comes from the thyroid itself, under TRH → TSH control. It has a half-life of about a week and is more than 99.9% protein-bound. Long-lived and almost entirely sequestered — that is a reservoir, not a messenger.

teach.h: T3 is the molecule that acts
teach.p: Most T3 is produced outside the thyroid, by 5'-deiodinase removing an iodine from T4. It is roughly three to four times more potent, with a half-life closer to a day. Both bind nuclear thyroid receptors, but T3 is the ligand that does the work.

Thyroid hormone raises the transcription of cardiac β1 receptors. The tachycardia and tremor of thyroid excess are not caused by extra catecholamines — measured catecholamine levels are normal or even low. They come from tissues made more sensitive to the catecholamines already present, which is why a β-blocker calms the symptoms without touching the thyroid.

Exogenous thyroid hormone suppresses TSH either way. But someone misusing T4 shows suppressed TSH with a high free T4, while someone misusing T3 alone shows suppressed TSH with a low free T4 — because the suppressed TSH removes the drive on their own gland, and that gland is the only source of T4. They are swallowing the active hormone while their thyroid stops making the precursor. On a screening panel that second pattern can read as central hypothyroidism, which is the opposite of what is happening — a free T3 settles it, and it will be high.

amine.title: Four ways to fake a sympathetic signal
amine.blurb: Direct, releaser, blocker, mixed — and one agent that is not adrenergic at all.

teach.p: Clenbuterol is a β2 agonist: it occupies the receptor directly, needing no nerve terminal, no transporter and no hypothalamic axis. Bronchodilation is the licensed veterinary use; the repartitioning effect that gets it abused is robust in livestock and far weaker in humans at doses people can tolerate.

teach.h: Releaser — force the terminal to dump
teach.p: Amphetamine is a substrate for DAT and NET. It reverses their transport direction and disrupts VMAT2 vesicular storage, so the neuron pours its own stores into the synapse. Nothing needs to bind the postsynaptic receptor — the transmitter is already there, in excess.

Methylphenidate blocks the same DAT and NET, and stops there. No transport reversal, no VMAT2 involvement, no release. It can only raise what is already being released, which is a genuinely different ceiling from amphetamine's — and releaser-versus-blocker is the discriminator most often tested on these two.

Ephedrine releases norepinephrine and adds weak direct agonism on top. Because part of its effect depends on releasable stores, repeated dosing shows tachyphylaxis as those stores run down — the classic teaching point for indirectly acting sympathomimetics. Direct agents fade too, but at the other end: clenbuterol keeps working until the β2 receptors themselves desensitise and downregulate, which is why it gets cycled rather than run continuously. Presynaptic depletion versus postsynaptic downregulation — same waning effect, opposite site.

teach.h: And one that is not adrenergic at all
teach.p: Caffeine antagonises A1 and A2A adenosine receptors. Adenosine accumulates with sustained activity and signals fatigue; blocking it lowers perceived effort. The target is the point: caffeine binds no adrenergic receptor and no monoamine transporter, so it enters the system through a completely different door from the other agents here. Downstream is another matter — A1 blockade disinhibits dopamine and norepinephrine release, striatal A2A receptors are coupled to D2, and at the top of the ergogenic range, around 6 mg/kg, plasma epinephrine does rise. At the bottom of it, it does not: 3 mg/kg improved time to exhaustion by the same ~22% with plasma epinephrine unchanged. The catecholamine rise travels alongside the effect rather than causing it. Separate entry point, overlapping destination.
